<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="The overall learning objectives for Module 5 are to: ​
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Apply California’s 5-Step CQI Process to prevention services
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Learn practical steps to integrate the 5-Step CQI Process into agency workflows
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Develop strategies to overcome common CQI implementation barriers" /> </Block> </Content> </Document>

<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="As a reminder from module 1, in child welfare, we are always striving for effective service delivery and positive outcomes for children, youth and families. Having a robust continuous quality improvement system in place significantly contributes to this effort. 
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="CQI is a proactive process that leverages data to improve services and child welfare outcomes – it is a systematic and structured approach that involves identifying, describing, and analyzing strengths and problems, uncovering the root causes of those problems, and then testing, and revising solutions that may solve those problems.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="In this definition:Testing and revising solutions means designing and implementing small tests of change and making course corrections based on what is learned.Organizational culture – refers to having a receptive environment where continuous learning is valued over punishment. CQI thrives best in a learning organization that values using data and evidence to understand and solve problems; It's also important to ensure there is clear understanding of mission, values, priorities, and desired outcomes across the organization and that you are collecting data and evidence that is aligned with those priorities to fuel and inform improvement efforts.A critical piece of CQI is active inclusion and participation from people with diverse experiences. That means staff at all levels, the children and youth served, parents and caregivers, people with lived experience, service providers, and community partners. Clear communication pathways should exist to share and act on performance information.And the Rigorous use of evidence – involves making meaning of data through robust analysis and putting the numbers into context." /> </Block> </Content> </Document>

<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="You may also remember this slide from module 1. I’m not going to read it all, but we have touched on some of these points. CQI has a lot of benefits!Select each character below to learn about the importance of CQI." /> </Block> </Content> </Document>

<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style FlowDirection="LeftToRight" TrailingMargin="0" LineSpacingRule="Single" LineSpacing="20"> <ListStyle ListType="None" ListTypeFormat="Parentheses" Color="#000000" BulletFont="Arial" /> </Style> <Span Text="As a reminder, where applicable, counties should establish a maximum of three CQI Implementation Teams: 
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style FlowDirection="LeftToRight" TrailingMargin="0" LineSpacingRule="Single" LineSpacing="20"> <ListStyle ListType="None" ListTypeFormat="Parentheses" Color="#000000" BulletFont="Arial" /> </Style> <Span Text="Home Visiting (HV) CQI Team: Designed to oversee the implementation of EBPs such as Healthy Families America (HFA), Nurse Family Partnership (NFP), Parents As Teachers (PAT), Homebuilders, and Family Check-Up. Motivational Interviewing (MI) CQI Team: Focused on supporting the implementation and fidelity monitoring of motivational interviewing. Mental Health (MH) CQI Team: Dedicated to overseeing the implementation of EBPs such as Parent Child Interaction Therapy (PCIT), Functional Family Therapy (FFT), Multisystemic Therapy (MST), and Brief Strategic Family Therapy (BSFT). 
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style FlowDirection="LeftToRight" TrailingMargin="0" LineSpacingRule="Single" LineSpacing="20"> <ListStyle ListType="None" ListTypeFormat="Parentheses" Color="#000000" BulletFont="Arial" /> </Style> <Span Text="Counties that do not establish separate teams must ensure that their existing CQI teams are structured to address the specific needs of EBP implementation. This may involve modifying members, meeting frequency, the agenda focus to ensure that CQI activities are meaningfully embedded into ongoing work. Regardless of structure, counties should ensure that these teams provide a dedicated space for monitoring EBP implementation and fidelity, identifying disparities, and driving continuous improvement.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style FlowDirection="LeftToRight" TrailingMargin="0" LineSpacingRule="Single" LineSpacing="20"> <ListStyle ListType="None" ListTypeFormat="Parentheses" Color="#000000" BulletFont="Arial" /> </Style> </Block> </Content> </Document>

<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style FlowDirection="LeftToRight" TrailingMargin="0" LineSpacingRule="Single" LineSpacing="20"> <ListStyle ListType="None" ListTypeFormat="Parentheses" BulletFont="Arial" /> </Style> <Span Text="The best practice recommendation in the CQI Plan is to establish dedicated CQI Implementation Teams aligned with the specific EBPs outlined in your county's and/or Tribe's CPP. This targeted approach supports fidelity and addresses challenges unique to each EBP. 
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style FlowDirection="LeftToRight" TrailingMargin="0" LineSpacingRule="Single" LineSpacing="20"> <ListStyle ListType="None" ListTypeFormat="Parentheses" BulletFont="Arial" /> </Style> <Span Text="This includes a maximum of three teams:Motivational Interviewing (MI) Home Visiting (HV) EBPs Mental Health (MH) EBPs 
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style FlowDirection="LeftToRight" TrailingMargin="0" LineSpacingRule="Single" LineSpacing="20"> <ListStyle ListType="None" ListTypeFormat="Parentheses" BulletFont="Arial" /> </Style> <Span Text="By aligning teams with specific EBPs, counties and tribes can better accomplish the purpose of identifying data trends, challenges, and opportunities for improvement in delivery of evidence-based practices.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style FlowDirection="LeftToRight" TrailingMargin="0" LineSpacingRule="Single" LineSpacing="20"> <ListStyle ListType="None" ListTypeFormat="Parentheses" BulletFont="Arial" /> </Style> <Span Text="County's and/or Tribe's FFPS CQI Teams have critical objectives focused on maintaining the CQI data infrastructure:Facilitate data collection & exchange for timely sharing of EBP data (reach, capacity, outcomes, fidelity) to inform decision-making across governance levels.-Review data regularly using CARES Dashboards to monitor progress, identify barriers, and make data-driven decisions.Analyze data and implement the 5-Step CQI Process to test changes, learn from outcomes, and implement sustainable improvements, driving continuous learning and system improvements.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style FlowDirection="LeftToRight" TrailingMargin="0" LineSpacingRule="Single" LineSpacing="20"> <ListStyle ListType="None" ListTypeFormat="Parentheses" BulletFont="Arial" /> </Style> <Span Text="Frequency of team meetings is tiered: During the first year, monthly meetings for each CQI team (max of three) or designate team are recommended to ensure consistent monitoring of reach and capacity data using the CARES dashboards and provider data. These initial meetings should focus on identifying implementation challenges, tracking progress, and making timely adjustments to address issues such as underutilization or disparities in service access. While outcome and fidelity data will only be formally collected biannually or annually for PAT, early review of available data is critical to inform timely decision-making and course corrections. In the second year, it is recommended that the meeting cadence shift to a quarterly schedule as counties move toward more in-depth analyses of EBP effectiveness and fidelity. This transition supports deeper evaluations of longer-term trends and outcomes, providing an opportunity to assess whether EBPs are achieving their intended goals and maintaining adherence to model standards. Capacity and reach data should continue to be reviewed regularly to monitor service accessibility and utilization, ensuring that counties remain responsive to family and community needs. After the second year, counties may adjust the frequency of team meetings on an ad hoc basis to address specific challenges or respond to emerging needs. This flexible approach enables counties to maintain a responsive CQI process while ensuring that data collection and analysis remain consistent and aligned with local and statewide goals. By adapting their meeting cadence over time, teams can sustain momentum while focusing on the most pressing issues at each stage of implementation. 
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style FlowDirection="LeftToRight" TrailingMargin="0" LineSpacingRule="Single" LineSpacing="20"> <ListStyle ListType="None" ListTypeFormat="Parentheses" BulletFont="Arial" /> </Style> <Span Text="Most importantly, each team should include a diverse set of members to ensure comprehensive decision-making and promote equity.Recommended members includes compensated Tribal representatives or advocates and compensated lived/community experts, county's and/or Tribe's child welfare and probation FFPS/CQI leads and county's and/or Tribe's child welfare and probation administrators, contract holders, and EBP providers (recognizing this may be impossible for large or medium size counties with multiple providers).Diverse membership isn’t just a checkbox—it ensures decisions are informed by real-world experiences and promotes equity through an inclusive approach.CDSS is committed to supporting counties in compensating Tribal representatives, lived experts, and community experts for their participation – more on this will be shared in coming months.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style FlowDirection="LeftToRight" TrailingMargin="0" LineSpacingRule="Single" LineSpacing="20"> <ListStyle ListType="None" ListTypeFormat="Parentheses" BulletFont="Arial" /> </Style> <Span Text="In the next lesson, we will learn more about the process of maintaining a CQI Data Infrastructure.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style FlowDirection="LeftToRight" TrailingMargin="0" LineSpacingRule="Single" LineSpacing="20"> <ListStyle ListType="None" ListTypeFormat="Parentheses" BulletFont="Arial" /> </Style> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style FlowDirection="LeftToRight" TrailingMargin="0" LineSpacingRule="Single" LineSpacing="20"> <ListStyle ListType="None" ListTypeFormat="Parentheses" BulletFont="Arial" /> </Style> </Block> </Content> </Document>

<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style FlowDirection="LeftToRight" TrailingMargin="0" LineSpacingRule="SinglePt5"> <ListStyle ListType="None" ListTypeFormat="Parentheses" Color="#000000" BulletFont="Arial" /> </Style> <Span Text="This slide should look familiar- it is California’s 5-Step CQI process. As a recap, step one is to define the problem, step two is understand the underlying conditions, step 3 is identify a solution and plan for implementation, step 4 is implementation of the solution, and step five is testing the solution and revise the approach as needed. " /> </Block> </Content> </Document>

<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="A metric is a number used to measure or track something specific.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Metrics help us understand how much, how many, or how often something is happening.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="In child welfare, metrics help agencies monitor workload, track outcomes, and identify trends.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Examples of metrics: number of new cases opened this week, average caseload size per worker, and number of children reunified with their families this year.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Metrics turn every day observations into numbers that can be compared tracked over time and shared with others." /> </Block> </Content> </Document>

<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="The most common quantitative metrics used to measure reach, capacity, fidelity, and outcomes in FFPS EBPs are counts, percents, and ratios. 
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="A count is the raw number of times something occurs within your population. (e.g. 78 children entered foster care last quarter)
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="A percent is a count divided by the total, multiplied by 100 — answers "out of every 100, how many?” (e.g. 42 out of 300 cases is 14%)
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="A ratio is a comparison of two quantities to each other. (e.g. for every 1 supervisor there are 8 caseworkers; or 2 out of every 5 cases involve children under age 5)
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Each metric type serves a different purpose — counts tell you how many, percents tell you how common, and ratios tell you how things compare." /> </Block> </Content> </Document>

<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="A data visualization is a chart, graph, or figure that turns numbers into a picture so patterns are easier to see. A bar chart compares counts or amounts across groups. A pie chart shows how a whole is divided into parts. A line chart typically tracks changes over time. A data table organizes metrics into rows and columns." /> </Block> </Content> </Document>

<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="A bar chart should answer four questions. “Who” meaning what population or populations are represented in the metric. In this case the " /> <Span Text="“" /> <Span Text="Who" /> <Span Text="”" /> <Span Text=" are staff and supervisors. The “what” meaning what metric is used and what outcome is being reported. The metric being reported here is the percent of staff and supervisors who have completed required trainings. " /> <Span Text="“" /> <Span Text="When" /> <Span Text="”" /> <Span Text=" should be added to the data visualization. Here you can see it in the title: Q1 of 2024. Finally, " /> <Span Text="“W" /> <Span Text="here" /> <Span Text="”" /> <Span Text=" should also be documented on a data visualization. Here it is also in the title: Flourishing Families of Monterey. What is not shown on this chart, but is also, important to note if you have the information is the data source and the date the data was pulled." /> </Block> </Content> </Document>

<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Now it is time to check your learning. Can you identify the who, what, when, and where on this bar chart?" /> </Block> </Content> </Document>
